card.title: Who Can Authorize This?
card.instruction: Treat titles and speeches as secondary; focus on who can grant access, allocate resources, and create consequences.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Lovely ribbon-cutting. Our freezer delivery is outside; who can unlock the building?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: The chief executive wants us both in the photograph first.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Can she let the freezers in? Photograph us while she unlocks.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Only the caretaker has keys. He's driving her home.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Keep her posing, then. I'll get the caretaker to open up before she needs her car.

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 seeks real building access rather than ceremony, A3 tests the executive's practical power, and A5 works through the caretaker who holds the keys.

responseLogic.evidence: B2's photograph demand informs A3's combined proposal; B4's driver-and-key information enables A5's posing delay.

relationship.evidence: B2 represents the ceremony's competing demand and B4 provides decisive operational information.

heightening.evidence: A5 uses B4's driving arrangement to keep the key holder available while the executive remains in the photograph.

specificity.evidence: A1 establishes an outside freezer delivery and B4 clearly identifies who can unlock the building.

brevityWit.evidence: A5's keep-her-posing tactic is earned by B4's exact account of the caretaker's dependency.
